What Does a Financial Advisor Do? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 9, 2026 A financial advisor typically gives you ongoing advice on buying, selling and holding investments and monitors how they perform. Investor.gov describes the service this way. Some advisers also give asset allocation advice or offer financial planning. If your money problem is debt, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) describes a different professional: the nonprofit credit counselor, who helps with budgets, debts and debt management plans. No primary source we read defines what a financial coach does, so with a coach you ask what that specific person provides. Tools for this journey All financial calculators → What a Financial Advisor Does for You A financial advisor gives you ongoing investment advice and monitors how your investments perform, according to Investor.gov, which spells the title "adviser". The services Investor.gov lists for investment advisers are: Ongoing advice about buying, selling or holding investments. Monitoring of how your investments perform. Checks that your investments still match your overall investment objectives. Advice about market trends or asset allocation, which some advisers offer. Financial planning services, which some advisers offer. Investor.gov presents the first three as what advisers typically provide and the last two as services an adviser "also may" offer. Ask each adviser which items on this list come with the account. Brokers overlap with advisers on part of this work. Investor.gov's page on Form CRS (the customer relationship summary) says both brokers and advisers can give advice about buying investments, such as stock in a company or an index fund, and about whether to sell or hold afterward. Many firms are registered as both a broker and an adviser (dual registrants), and Investor.gov says a combination of advisory and brokerage accounts may be a good choice depending on your goals, preferences and needs. Before a first meeting, write down which of the five services above you want. Then compare that list with what each advisor says it provides. Financial Advisor Fees and How Advisors Get Paid An investment adviser's fee is typically based on the value of all the assets held in your account with that adviser, according to Investor.gov. You may also pay other fees and costs for servicing the account and for the investments you buy, sell or hold. Investor.gov does not publish typical fee percentages on its Investment Advisers page, so ask each adviser for every fee and cost in writing. Investor.gov says investment advisers are required to act in your best interest and not put their interest ahead of yours. The same page says the way advisers make money creates some conflicts with your interests, and those conflicts can affect the investment advice you receive. Our guide to what a fiduciary is covers that best-interest duty on its own. A relationship summary shows what a pay disclosure looks like on paper. One firm's Form CRS answers the question "How do your financial professionals make money?" by saying it pays its financial professionals in different ways, including commissions and advisory fees. The same firm says higher commissions, costs or fees could lead to higher pay for a financial professional, which is the kind of conflict Investor.gov tells you to ask about. Advisor, Credit Counselor and Coach Roles Compared A financial advisor, a nonprofit credit counselor and a financial coach do different jobs, and Investor.gov and the CFPB describe only the first two. Role What the sources say Who it fits What to ask Investment adviser Ongoing advice on buying, selling or holding investments, plus monitoring. Some add asset allocation advice or financial planning (Investor.gov) Someone who wants help with investments over time How is your fee calculated, which services are included, and what conflicts do you have? Nonprofit credit counselor Advice on money and debts, budget help, debt management plans and money management workshops. Counselors certified and trained in consumer credit, debt management and budgeting (CFPB) Someone whose main problem is debt or a budget What does each service cost, in writing, and how are your employees paid? Financial coach No primary source we read defines the job. Coach titles appear in a credentials database covered below Not described by any source we read What exactly do you provide, what does it cost, and what registration or designation do you hold? Under a debt management plan, the CFPB says, you make a single payment to the credit counseling organization each month or pay period, and the organization pays each of your creditors. The CFPB says such a plan typically lowers monthly payments, interest charges and fees. The National Foundation for Credit Counseling (NFCC) describes credit counseling that starts with a confidential consultation and a personalized action plan. It lists more than 1,500 NFCC certified credit counselors. Coach and counselor titles appear in the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) professional designations database . Examples are Certified Financial and Career Coach (CFCC), Certified Workplace Money Coach (CWMC), Certified Professional Retirement Coach (CPRC), Accredited Financial Counselor (AFC) and Certified Financial Counselor (CFC). FINRA says it does not approve or endorse any professional credential or designation, so a listing in that database is not a FINRA endorsement of the title. Investor.gov warns that initials after a broker's or adviser's name do not make that person more qualified than another, and they do not necessarily mean better service for you. Some initials may mean the person can sell only certain products, and the FINRA list shows that some credentials are easy to obtain while others are hard-earned. If you are weighing an advisor against a planner, our financial advisor vs financial planner comparison covers that pair. How to Check Who You Are Talking To Investor.gov says the most important question before you hire an investment professional is whether that person is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) or with a state securities regulator. Its Working with an Investment Professional page calls it "really risky" to invest with someone who isn't licensed. The same page points to a free search tool. It shows whether a professional is licensed and registered. Registered broker-dealers and registered investment advisers are required to give retail investors a Form CRS. Investor.gov says each one covers: The types of services the firm offers. The fees and costs you will pay. Conflicts of interest a broker or adviser may have. The required standard of conduct for the services. Whether the firm and its financial professionals have reportable legal or disciplinary history. Conversation starters, which are questions to ask. These summaries use similar headings in a similar order, so you can set two firms' summaries side by side and compare them topic by topic. Investor.gov's checklist for selecting an adviser adds questions of your own: what services and products you need, any limits on what the adviser can provide, and, if there is legal or disciplinary history, what type of conduct it involved. Our guide on how to choose a financial advisor covers that selection process. Credit counselors come with a different checklist from the CFPB. The CFPB says a reputable organization should send free information without asking for details about your situation, and if it will not, you should go elsewhere. It also tells you to: Get a specific price quote in writing. Read anything before you sign it. Avoid any organization that pushes a debt management plan as your only option before it analyzes your situation. Ask whether the counselor is accredited or certified, what training the counselor has, and how employees are paid. The CFPB's credit counseling page also names your state attorney general and state consumer protection agency as places to check on an organization. Who a Financial Advisor Is Not For and What Would Change the Answer Our read is that an advisor is the wrong first call if your main problem is debt or a budget. The CFPB describes nonprofit credit counselors as the people who advise on money and debts, help with budgets, develop debt management plans and offer money management workshops. Investor.gov describes the typical adviser relationship as ongoing advice paid through a fee based on your account assets, so ask any advisor you contact whether it offers anything shorter and what that costs, in writing. If the question is whether the ongoing fee pays for itself, our guide on whether a financial advisor is worth it handles that decision. Our answer would change if the rules behind it changed. Everything above about advisers rests on Investor.gov's description of a best-interest duty, fees typically tied to assets and the Form CRS requirement, so a change to adviser registration or disclosure rules would change what you can expect. For coaches, our answer would change if a primary source published a definition of the job, and until one does, the description of a coach's work to rely on is the one that coach gives you in writing. Our Takeaway A financial advisor typically gives and monitors investment advice for a fee usually tied to the assets in your account, and some advisers add asset allocation advice or financial planning. A nonprofit credit counselor helps with budgets, debts and debt management plans, and for a financial coach you ask what exactly that person provides. If your need is debt help, the CFPB describes nonprofit credit counselors who help with budgets and debts. Write down the job you need done, then ask each candidate, in writing, which services they provide and how they are paid. Frequently asked questions What does a financial advisor do for you? A financial advisor typically gives you ongoing advice about buying, selling or holding investments, according to Investor.gov. The adviser also monitors how those investments perform against your overall objectives. Some advisers also give advice on market trends or asset allocation, or offer financial planning services. The fee is typically based on the value of the assets in your account with that adviser. What should a financial advisor do for me? A financial advisor should act in your best interest and not put their interest ahead of yours, which Investor.gov says investment advisers are required to do. Beyond that duty, services vary by adviser. Investor.gov suggests comparing what you need with what the adviser provides, any limits, what you will pay, how the adviser gets paid and what conflicts the adviser has. The adviser's Form CRS lists services, fees, conflicts and any reportable legal or disciplinary history in a standard order. Is credit counseling free? Credit counseling is not always free. The CFPB says most credit counseling organizations are non-profits, yet credit counselors may charge fees for some of their services. A reputable organization should send you free information without asking for details about your situation, and you should get a specific price quote in writing before you sign anything. Do I need a financial advisor? It depends on whether you want ongoing advice about buying, selling and holding investments, which Investor.gov says an adviser typically provides for a fee based on the value of the assets in your account. Our guide on whether a financial advisor is worth it weighs that cost against the value. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. The wording below comes from the Form CRS of one firm registered as both a broker-dealer and an investment adviser, retrieved on November 9, 2026. Under each question is what a clear answer should cover. "Given my financial situation, should I choose an investment advisory service? Should I choose a brokerage service? Should I choose both types of services? Why or why not?" The Investor.gov Form CRS page says brokers and advisers can both advise on buying a stock or an index fund and on whether to sell or hold it later. A clear answer explains which type of service, or which combination, fits your goals, preferences and needs. "How will you choose investments to recommend to me?" The Investor.gov investment advisers page says an adviser typically gives ongoing advice and monitors how your investments perform and how they line up with your overall objectives. A clear answer says what the person looks at when picking an investment and how they review it afterward. "What is your relevant experience, including your licenses, education and other qualifications? What do these qualifications mean?" Investor.gov warns that initials after a name do not make one person more qualified than another, and that some initials mean the person can only sell certain products. A clear answer names each credential and says what it lets the person sell or do for you. "Help me understand how these fees and costs might affect my investments. If I give you $10,000 to invest, how much will go to fees and costs, and how much will be invested for me?" The Form CRS notes that fees and costs reduce what you make on your investments over time, and that you pay them whether you make or lose money. "What are your legal obligations to me when providing recommendations as my broker-dealer or when acting as my investment adviser?" Investor.gov says investment advisers are required to act in your best interest and not put their interest ahead of yours. A clear answer states the duty for each role the person could play with your account, and our guide on what a fiduciary is explains the adviser side of that duty. "How else does your firm make money, and what conflicts of interest do you have?" Follow it with the form's own prompt: "How might your conflicts of interest affect me, and how will you address them?" Investor.gov says the way advisers make money creates some conflicts with your interests, and those conflicts can affect the advice you get. A clear answer names each conflict and what the firm does about it. "How do your financial professionals make money?" The firm whose form is quoted here says it pays its financial professionals in different ways, including commissions and advisory fees, and that higher commissions, costs or fees could lead to higher pay for the professional. That is one firm's disclosure, so ask the person in front of you to describe their own pay. "As a financial professional, do you have any disciplinary history? For what type of conduct?" Investor.gov says a Form CRS has to state whether the firm and its financial professionals have reportable legal or disciplinary history. A clear answer matches what the form says and explains the conduct behind any entry. Ask for the answers in writing where you can. Then compare the written answers with the firm's Form CRS after the meeting. Public Record Checks on Registration and History The answers about registration and disciplinary history can be checked against public records before you hire anyone. Investor.gov calls registration with the SEC or a state securities regulator the most important question to settle first. Its Working with an Investment Professional page offers a free and simple search that shows whether an investment professional is licensed and registered. You can also run a name through adviserinfo.sec.gov and through BrokerCheck from the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) . If the person lists the Certified Financial Planner (CFP) credential, look the name up on the CFP Board's verification page . Investor.gov also points to a FINRA list showing that some credentials are easy to obtain and others are hard-earned. Next, set the person's spoken answers beside the firm's Form CRS . Investor.gov says every relationship summary covers the firm's services, fees and costs, conflicts of interest, required standard of conduct, and legal or disciplinary history, using similar headings and order of topics. If a spoken fee or conflict answer does not match the form, ask which one is correct and get the reply in writing. Our guide on how to choose a financial advisor covers the wider comparison between firms once each candidate has answered the same eight questions. Red Flags and What To Do Three situations are reasons to look at other candidates. The first rests on Investor.gov's warning. The other two are our judgment, built on what Form CRS must contain. The person is not registered with the SEC or a state securities regulator. Investor.gov says it is "really risky to invest with someone who isn't licensed," so move on to another candidate. The firm will not give you a Form CRS. Registered broker-dealers and registered investment advisers are required to give one to retail investors, so ask once in writing and keep looking if it still does not arrive. The record shows legal or disciplinary history the person cannot explain. Investor.gov lists that history, and the type of conduct behind it, among the things to weigh before selecting an adviser. We would treat an entry the person cannot explain as a reason to choose someone else. A clean record does not settle the other questions on the list. Keep the fee, duty and conflict answers in your comparison even for a candidate with no history. Questions To Ask a Financial Advisor in Special Situations If you want more than investment recommendations, add questions about planning services and about which accounts and products the person can offer. Investor.gov says advisers may also give advice about market trends or asset allocation, or offer financial planning services. It also tells you to weigh the services and products you need against what the adviser can provide and any limits on it. Do you offer financial planning services, or advice on asset allocation? Which services and products can you provide, and what can you not provide? Can your firm offer both advisory and brokerage accounts? Investor.gov notes that many firms are registered as both a broker and an adviser and offer both types of account. How much will I pay for services, and how much for each transaction? For retirement savings, use the same eight questions and add which retirement account types the person handles. Retirement account rules and contribution limits are outside these questions. Who These Questions Are Not For and What Would Change the List These questions fit someone choosing an ongoing relationship with an adviser or broker. Investor.gov says advisers typically provide ongoing advice, and that the adviser's fee is typically based on the value of all the assets in your account, with other fees and costs possible on top. If you need only a one-time answer to a single money question, read our guide on whether a financial advisor is worth it before you sit through a full interview. Two things would change this list. If the SEC changes the conversation starters printed on Form CRS, we would rebuild the list from the new form. If a candidate fails the registration question, you can skip the rest of the list for that person, because Investor.gov treats registration as the first test. Our Takeaway Ask every candidate the same eight questions listed above, then compare their written answers with the firm's own Form CRS and their public record. Look elsewhere if the person is not registered or cannot explain a disciplinary record. The same list works whether the person is an investment adviser, a broker or part of a firm that is both. Copy these questions to ask a financial advisor, send them before the first meeting, and check the person's registration with the free search on Investor.gov . What Is a Robo-Advisor? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 9, 2026 A robo-advisor is an automated digital investment advisory program that builds and manages an investment portfolio for you from your answers to an online questionnaire. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) explains the model in an Investor Bulletin on robo-advisers, and the Investor.gov glossary defines the term. The questionnaire asks about your financial goals, investment horizon, income, other assets and risk tolerance. Robo-advisors often aim to charge lower costs and fees than traditional advisory programs. Some require lower account minimums. In exchange, some robo-advisors offer little or no contact with a person, and the advice can only use what the questionnaire collects. Tools for this journey All financial calculators → What a Robo-Advisor Is and Who It Fits A robo-advisor fits you if you are comfortable answering an online questionnaire, reading its disclosures online and working with limited human contact. It does not fit you if you want to speak with a person during a market downturn, or if your finances include debts and assets its questionnaire does not ask about. Investor.gov spells the term "robo-adviser" and describes it as an automated digital investment advisory program. In most cases it collects your financial goals, investment horizon, income, other assets and risk tolerance through an online questionnaire. "Based on that information, it creates and manages an investment portfolio for you," the Investor.gov glossary entry says. The same entry says services, approaches and features vary widely. Two robo-advisors can differ in what they ask you, what they invest in and how much human help they offer. The SEC Investor Bulletin on robo-advisers , published February 23, 2017, asks readers to weigh how much human interaction matters to them and to consider their own level of financial literacy. How a Robo-Advisor Works A robo-advisor lets you create and manage your investment account through a web portal or mobile application, sometimes with little or no interaction with a human being. You answer the questionnaire. The robo-advisor uses those answers to build and manage your portfolio. The SEC bulletin names lower costs than traditional advisory programs as the potential benefit of that setup. The SEC bulletin says a robo-advisor's recommendation is limited by the information it requests and receives from you. Some robo-advisors obtain and consider only limited information. In many cases the burden to update that information falls on you. Investing approaches differ from one robo-advisor to the next. Some offer several pre-determined portfolios that you may or may not be able to customize. Others use a limited range of products, such as broad-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The SEC bulletin says a robo-advisor's services, approaches and features are described in its Form ADV Part 1 and Part 2 brochure. Hybrid, Limited or No Human Contact The amount of human contact varies from one robo-advisor to the next, and the SEC bulletin describes three arrangements. Hybrid advice, sometimes called "bionic" advice, where you can contact an investment professional in addition to using the automated service. Access to a person only for accounts that meet a minimum size. Technical support staff only, with no investment professional to contact. Unlike a traditional adviser, a robo-advisor may have no initial or later conversation with you to gather information about your needs. The SEC bulletin asks whether you would like to speak with a person during market events such as downturns. If your answer is yes, put hybrid access on your list of requirements and ask what account size it needs. If you would rather work with a person from the start, our guide on how to choose a financial advisor walks through that search. What to Check Before You Open an Account The SEC bulletin poses questions to ask before you open a robo-advisor account, and they fit into six checks. What information it uses. The bulletin suggests asking whether the questionnaire covers high-interest credit card debt or student loans, bank and savings accounts, real estate holdings, retirement accounts and other assets. Anything it does not ask about stays outside the advice. How it handles risk and rebalancing. The bulletin suggests asking how the robo-advisor takes your risk tolerance into account, including when it rebalances after a market decline, and how often it rebalances your account. Rebalancing can have tax implications, and some robo-advisors may be able to freeze sales during market volatility. Which account types it manages. The bulletin lists individual retirement accounts (IRAs), taxable accounts, 401(k) plans and college savings accounts as types to ask about. Whether it uses tax loss harvesting. The bulletin says its value depends on your tax situation and that it may implicate wash-sale rules, so it suggests considering a tax adviser. Your total costs. The bulletin says fees and other costs can greatly impact your return. A robo-advisor may offer lower-cost advice, but if it uses high-cost investment products, your total costs could still be high. Its registration. Investor.gov calls registration with the SEC or a state securities regulator the most important question before hiring an investment professional, and robo-advisers are investment advisers. Search the firm at adviserinfo.sec.gov before you open an account. The bulletin adds that in some cases a robo-advisor may offer services that are not much different from a traditional advisory program or from a single product such as a target date retirement fund. Investor.gov warns that investing with someone who isn't licensed is "really risky" and offers a free search tool that shows whether an investment professional is licensed and registered. Who a Robo-Advisor Does Not Fit Our guide on whether a financial advisor is worth it compares a robo-advisor with a human advisor. The SEC bulletin also notes that in some cases robo-advisers may not have been tested under stressed market conditions. If you want a person to talk to during a downturn, a robo-advisor that offers only technical support leaves you without one. Add up total costs first Investor.gov glossary, SEC bulletin Our answer changes in two cases. If a robo-advisor's questionnaire asks about your debts, real estate and outside retirement accounts, the information objection shrinks. If it offers a hybrid human adviser, or a person for accounts above a minimum size you meet, the downturn objection shrinks. Our best robo-advisors roundup ranks individual providers. Our Takeaway A robo-advisor fits an investor who is comfortable with an online questionnaire, online disclosures and limited human contact. It does not fit someone who wants a person during market stress, or whose finances a questionnaire cannot capture, unless the provider offers a hybrid human adviser. This read rests on the Investor.gov glossary and the SEC's 2017 investor bulletin. Once you know what a robo-advisor is, run the six checks above on each provider you are considering. Start by searching the firm at adviserinfo.sec.gov , then ask for its Form ADV Part 2 brochure and compare providers in our best robo-advisors list . Frequently asked questions Are robo advisors good? A robo-advisor can be a good fit when you are comfortable with an online questionnaire, online disclosures and limited human contact. Investor.gov names the benefits: advice that often costs less than traditional advisory programs and, in some cases, lower account minimums. The SEC bulletin names the limits: advice bounded by what the questionnaire asks, human contact that varies by provider and, in some cases, no testing under stressed market conditions. Is a robo advisor worth it? A robo-advisor is worth it when its lower cost holds up after you add the advice fee to the cost of the investment products it uses, and when you do not need a person to talk to. The SEC bulletin warns that total costs can still be high if a robo-advisor uses high-cost products. It also says some robo-advisors offer services not much different from a traditional advisory program or a target date retirement fund. Why do some people say robo advisors are bad? The SEC bulletin lists three limits behind that view. A robo-advisor's recommendation is limited by the information its questionnaire collects, and keeping that information current is often up to you. Some offer only technical support staff, with no investment professional to call during a downturn. In some cases, robo-advisers may not have been tested under stressed market conditions. Is a robo-advisor a fiduciary? A robo-advisor is an investment adviser, and Investor.gov says investment advisers are required to act in your best interest and not put their interest ahead of yours. Investor.gov also says the way advisers make money creates some conflicts with your interests, so ask any robo-advisor about those conflicts. Our guide on what a fiduciary is explains the term. What Is a Certified Financial Planner (CFP)? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 9, 2026 A certified financial planner (CFP) professional is a financial planner that the Certified Financial Planner Board of Standards (CFP Board) has certified after four requirements. A CFP professional must also act as a fiduciary when giving you financial advice. The CFP Board calls the four requirements the "4 E's": Education, Exam, Experience and Ethics. In practice that means financial planning coursework plus a bachelor's degree, a 170-question exam, 6,000 hours of experience (or 4,000 apprenticeship hours) and a signed Ethics Declaration. The degree can be finished up to five years after the exam, and the experience hours can come before or after it. Tools for this journey All financial calculators → What a Certified Financial Planner Is and What It Takes to Earn It A CFP professional is a financial planner who has met the CFP Board's four requirements (education, exam, experience and ethics) and who must act as a fiduciary when giving financial advice. The CFP Board allows the bachelor's degree to be finished up to five years after the exam, so a planner can pass the exam before holding the degree. The fiduciary duty comes from the CFP Board's Code of Ethics and Standards of Conduct . The Code reads: "At all times when providing Financial Advice to a Client, a CFP professional must act as a fiduciary, and therefore, act in the best interests of the Client." Earning the credential follows a set order. Coursework comes first, because the CFP Board requires it before you can take the exam. The experience hours can land before or after the exam, and the Ethics Declaration is the final step. If you are deciding whom to hire, the credential tells you two things. The person met the CFP Board's education, exam and experience requirements. The person also agreed to put your best interests first when giving you financial advice. The Four CFP Certification Requirements in Detail The CFP Board's certification process page sets out four requirements, and each one has its own timing rule. Requirement What the CFP Board requires Timing Education Coursework through a CFP Board Registered Program, plus a bachelor's degree or higher in any discipline from an accredited college or university Coursework before the exam (average 12 to 18 months). Degree within 5 years after passing Exam 170 multiple-choice questions in two 3-hour sessions over one day After the coursework Experience 6,000 hours of professional experience related to the financial planning process, or 4,000 apprenticeship hours that meet additional requirements From 10 years before to 5 years after passing the exam Ethics Sign the Ethics Declaration. A background check is among the final requirements Final step Education has two parts. The coursework must come through a CFP Board Registered Program, and the CFP Board puts the average time to finish it at 12 to 18 months. The degree can be in any discipline, as long as it is a bachelor's or higher from an accredited college or university. The exam runs two 3-hour sessions on one day, which adds up to 6 hours of testing. It mixes stand-alone questions, scenario-based questions and questions tied to case studies. All 170 questions are multiple choice. Experience has two paths. The standard path is 6,000 hours of professional experience related to the financial planning process. The apprenticeship path asks for 4,000 hours, which is 2,000 fewer, but those hours must meet additional requirements. The experience window opens 10 years before the exam and closes 5 years after it, so the hours must fall inside a 15-year span. The CFP Board says the experience requirement prepares a planner to provide personal financial planning to the public without supervision. Passing the exam completes one of the four requirements, and certification needs all four. The Seven Practice Standards a Certified Financial Planner Follows The CFP Board Code lists seven practice standards, and their headings describe the planning work a CFP professional does with a client. The planner works to understand your personal and financial circumstances. The planner identifies and selects goals. The planner analyzes your current course of action and potential alternative courses of action. The planner develops the financial planning recommendation or recommendations. The planner presents the financial planning recommendation or recommendations. The planner implements the financial planning recommendation or recommendations. The planner monitors progress and updates. You can turn the seven headings into first-meeting questions that test whether a planner follows each standard. Ask how the planner will learn your circumstances, how goals get selected, and how the planner will monitor progress and update the plan. The Fiduciary Commitment and Its Limits The CFP Board's ethics requirement commits a CFP professional to act as a fiduciary when providing financial advice to a client, always putting the client's best interests first. The certification process page calls this the final step on the path to certification. It says signing the Ethics Declaration shows the planner agreed to adhere to high ethical and professional standards for the practice of financial planning. The credential describes competence and conduct for financial advice. The credential does not set one way to be paid. The CFP Board Code requires a CFP professional giving financial advice to tell you before or at the engagement how you pay and how the professional and firm are compensated. Registration as an adviser or broker must still be checked separately. Our financial advisor vs. financial planner comparison covers those titles. Investor.gov says the most important question before hiring an investment professional is whether the person is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) or with a state securities regulator. Investor.gov warns that it is "really risky to invest with someone who isn't licensed." It offers a free and simple search tool that shows whether an investment professional is licensed and registered. Investor.gov also has a "Tricky Titles" warning. It says not to assume that initials after a broker's or adviser's name make that person more qualified than another, because the titles are not all the same and do not necessarily mean better service for you. The initials may even mean the person can sell only certain products, and Investor.gov points to a Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) list showing that some credentials are easy to obtain and others are hard-earned. Pay is the question the CFP initials leave open, so ask the person directly. J.P. Morgan Securities LLC's Form CRS (Client Relationship Summary), for example, says it pays its financial professionals in different ways, including commissions and advisory fees. It also says higher commissions, costs or fees could lead to higher compensation for a financial professional. Our guide to choosing a financial advisor lists more questions to ask before you hire anyone. Where the CFA and CTFA Credentials Fit Our guide to the CFA credential covers the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) designation. Our guide to the CTFA credential covers the Certified Trust and Fiduciary Advisor (CTFA) designation. If you need only trust administration, start with the CTFA guide. If you need only investment analysis, start with the CFA guide. Our answer rests on the CFP Board's requirements as listed on its certification process page. If the CFP Board changes its education, exam, experience or ethics rules, the steps described here change too. The CFP Board certification process page shows the current version. Our Takeaway A CFP professional has met four published requirements from the CFP Board and has committed to act as a fiduciary when giving financial advice. The credential signals planning competence, but not how the person is paid or registered, which you still verify. This takeaway rests on the CFP Board's published rules and Investor.gov guidance, and it shifts if you need only trust work or only investment analysis. Before you hire a certified financial planner, look the person up on the CFP Board verification page and run the registration search on Investor.gov or adviserinfo.sec.gov . Frequently asked questions What does a CFP do? A CFP professional follows the seven practice standards in the CFP Board Code. They are understanding your personal and financial circumstances, identifying and selecting goals, analyzing your current course of action and alternatives, developing recommendations, presenting them, implementing them, and monitoring progress and updating. Whenever the planner gives you financial advice, the Code requires the planner to act as a fiduciary in your best interests. How do CFPs get paid? The CFP credential does not set one way to be paid. The CFP Board Code requires a CFP professional giving financial advice to tell you before or at the engagement how you pay and how the professional and firm are compensated. J.P. Morgan Securities LLC's Form CRS, for example, says it pays its financial professionals in different ways, including commissions and advisory fees. The same form says higher commissions, costs or fees could lead to higher compensation for a financial professional, and that is one firm's disclosure rather than a rule for every firm. Is a CFP worth it? A CFP is worth looking for if you want a planner who has met the CFP Board's education, exam, experience and ethics requirements and has committed to act as a fiduciary when giving financial advice. The credential does not set how the person is paid, and registration as an adviser or broker still has to be verified separately. Look up registration with the search tool on Investor.gov before you hire. How do I become a CFP? You become a CFP professional by meeting the CFP Board's four requirements. Finish coursework through a CFP Board Registered Program (12 to 18 months on average), then pass the 170-question exam. Earn a bachelor's degree within five years of passing, log 6,000 experience hours or 4,000 apprenticeship hours, and sign the Ethics Declaration, as the certification process page lays out. One early piece to build is an emergency fund, a cash reserve for surprise costs such as a car repair or a medical bill. If you also carry high-interest debt, weigh paying it down alongside that reserve while you set up the rest of the plan. Tools for this journey All financial calculators → How to Make a Financial Plan Step by Step You can make a financial plan by running the seven-step process that the Certified Financial Planner Board of Standards (CFP Board) sets out in its practice standards, with you acting as both planner and client. One early action is an emergency fund, which the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) calls "one of the first steps you can take to start saving." If you carry high-interest debt too, weigh it alongside that reserve, because neither the CFP Board standards nor the CFPB emergency fund guide ranks one ahead of the other. We adapted the CFP Board's seven practice standards into household tasks. The wording of the tasks is ours, not CFP Board guidance, and the table below lists the seven tasks beside the standard each comes from. CFP Board practice standard What you do on your own Understanding the Client's Personal and Financial Circumstances List income, spending, savings, debts, insurance and estate documents Identifying and Selecting Goals Set goals with an amount and a date Analyzing the Client's Current Course of Action and Potential Alternative Courses of Action Compare your current course with other options Developing the Financial Planning Recommendation(s) Choose the changes you will make Presenting the Financial Planning Recommendation(s) Write the plan down and share it with anyone it affects Implementing the Financial Planning Recommendation(s) Carry out the changes, such as starting an emergency fund Monitoring Progress and Updating Review on a set date and update the plan The CFP Board expanded its process from six steps to seven. A planner develops a recommendation and then presents it to the client. On your own, those two standards become choosing your changes and writing them down. The Snapshot You Need to Make a Financial Plan A financial plan starts with a written record of your money today, because the CFP Board's first standard covers gathering both numbers and personal facts about the person being planned for. The CFP Board gives these examples of what a planner collects. Each one becomes a line in your snapshot: Income: each paycheck and any other money that arrives during the month. Expenses: what leaves your account, including bills that come once or twice a year. Savings: the balance in each savings account. Assets: what you own, such as a home, a car or retirement accounts. Liabilities: every debt, with its balance and interest rate. Insurance coverage: the health, auto, home or renters, life and disability policies you hold. Estate plans: any will or beneficiary forms you have on file. The CFP Board's list also covers your goals, your priorities and your risk tolerance. Write a sentence or two on each. The CFP Board offers these as examples of what a planner gathers, so add anything else that touches your money. To total the assets and liabilities above, use our net worth guide . Dated Goals and a Test of Your Current Course The CFPB's emergency fund guide builds a savings habit around three moves: set a goal, make consistent contributions and monitor progress. Use those same three moves for every goal you write down. Write each goal as one line: what it is, how much it costs and when you want it. Then run the CFP Board's third standard, which compares your current course of action with alternative courses. In plain terms, ask where your money ends up if nothing changes. To test a goal, use simple arithmetic: Subtract what you have already saved toward the goal from its amount. Divide what is left by the number of months until your date. Compare that monthly figure with what you set aside now. If the monthly figure is higher than your current saving, sketch one or two alternatives. You could save more each month, cut an expense or move the date later. Our financial planning calculator turns your income and goals into a savings rate, retirement-readiness or net worth number, so you can run each alternative. When goals compete for the same dollars, rank them with the priorities you wrote in your snapshot. The CFPB's Your Money, Your Goals toolkit offers free tools for setting goals and working through money challenges. An Emergency Fund as an Early Step An emergency fund is a cash reserve set aside for unplanned expenses or financial emergencies, such as car repairs, home repairs, medical bills or a loss of income, according to the CFPB. The CFPB calls setting one up one of the first steps you can take to start saving. It also says even a small amount helps you recover quicker and stay on track toward larger savings goals. The CFPB says how much you need depends on your situation. To set your own target, list the most common unexpected expenses you have had and what each one cost, then set a goal from that total. If you are living paycheck to paycheck, the CFPB notes that putting any money aside can feel difficult. It adds that even a small amount can provide some financial security. The CFPB lists these ways to build the reserve: Create a savings habit: set a goal, make consistent contributions and monitor your progress. Manage your cash flow. Put away a portion of your tax refund. Set up automatic recurring transfers, which the CFPB calls often one of the easiest ways to save. Pick the one you can start this week. High-Interest Debt Alongside the Reserve Neither the CFP Board standards nor the CFPB emergency fund guide ranks paying down high-interest debt against building a cash reserve, so you decide the order inside your own plan. Your snapshot already lists each debt with its balance and rate. In the course-testing step, write out two versions of the plan: one that sends extra money to the debt first, and one that builds the reserve first. Compare where each version leaves you by your goal dates. If the comparison does not settle it, a nonprofit credit counselor can look at your specifics, and the CFPB explains what credit counseling is . A financial professional can also work through the trade-off with you. Carrying Out and Reviewing Your Financial Plan A financial plan changes your money only after you carry it out, and the CFP Board's last two standards are implementing the recommendations and monitoring progress and updating. Turn each change into a task with a date. Open the savings account, set the automatic transfer and list the debt you will pay extra on. Then put a review date on your calendar. Choose one you will keep, such as the week you file your taxes, and add an extra review when your income, household or debts change. At each review, update your snapshot, check each goal against its date and adjust the plan. Who this is not for: a household with complex tax, estate or business questions, which may need a professional. Our guides on what a CFP is and how to choose a financial advisor cover that decision. Our answer would change if the CFP Board revised its seven practice standards or the CFPB published new emergency fund guidance. Our Takeaway Treat a financial plan as a repeating cycle: list your finances, set dated goals, test your current course, act, then review. Start an emergency fund early, as the CFPB suggests. If you carry high-interest debt, compare a debt-first and a reserve-first version of the plan before you choose. Households with complex tax, estate or investment questions may need a professional to run the same steps with them. Write down your income, spending, savings and debts today. Pick one goal with an amount and a date, and you can make a financial plan you can start this week. Frequently asked questions What should a financial plan include? A financial plan should include a written record of your income, expenses, savings, assets, liabilities, insurance coverage and estate plans, plus your goals, priorities and risk tolerance. The CFP Board gives these as examples of what a planner gathers. The plan then adds the actions from the later steps: the changes you chose, how you will carry them out and when you will review them. What are the components of a financial plan? The components of a financial plan are the facts you gather and the actions you choose, organized by the seven steps in the CFP Board's planning process. The facts include income, expenses, savings, assets, liabilities, insurance, estate plans, goals, priorities and risk tolerance. The actions cover goals, testing, changes, carrying out and review. Why make a financial plan? A financial plan gives each goal an amount, a date and a monthly action, so you can see whether your current course reaches it. The CFPB says even a small emergency fund helps you recover quicker from unplanned expenses and stay on track toward larger savings goals. Do I need a financial planner to make a plan? No rule in the CFP Board's standards or the CFPB's emergency fund guidance requires you to hire a planner to make a financial plan. The CFP Board's seven practice standards describe the process a planner follows, and you can adapt the same steps yourself. If your situation includes complex tax, estate or business questions, see our guide on what a CFP is before you decide whether to hire help. Some advisors are fiduciaries, meaning they must put your interests first. Others, such as brokers, follow Regulation Best Interest, a separate SEC standard for broker-dealers. This guide covers the standards, fee models, the CFP credential, how to verify an advisor, and what to ask during your first call. Tools for this journey What is a registered investment advisor → Retirement → Investing → Net worth → What is a CTFA → Know Which Type of Financial Professional You're Talking To "Financial advisor" is a loose umbrella term, and the specific job title someone uses often says more about how they're paid and regulated than the word "advisor" itself does. An investment adviser registers with the SEC or a state regulator and owes you the fiduciary duty covered in Step 1 below, typically charging a fee tied to the assets under management. A broker-dealer representative can also call themselves a financial advisor, but is held to Regulation Best Interest, a separate SEC standard for broker-dealers, and is often paid a commission on what they sell. A few other titles are worth naming directly. A wealth advisor usually follows the same fiduciary model as an investment adviser, aimed at higher-net-worth clients with higher account minimums . A financial coach or financial counselor may offer many kinds of help, so ask what that specific person provides. A CPA who also advises on investments needs a separate license to do so legally, since the CPA credential itself covers tax and accounting work, not investment management. A robo-advisor replaces the human with an algorithm that builds and rebalances a portfolio automatically, usually at a much lower fee. Our robo-advisor vs. financial advisor breakdown covers when that trade-off makes sense. Two more titles show up mostly at larger firms or in specific situations. A portfolio or asset manager runs the investment decisions inside a fund or a large account. That person often never speaks directly to the end client, since a financial advisor is usually the relationship-facing role sitting between that manager and you. A financial therapist works on the emotional and behavioral side of money instead, like anxiety around spending or conflict with a partner over finances. That role typically isn't licensed to manage investments or give specific investment advice at all. The CFP credential from Step 3 below cuts across most of these titles, and so does the related but less common ChFC (Chartered Financial Consultant) designation. Each is a personal qualification a person earns, separate from which of the business models above they actually work under. A CFP or ChFC can work as a fee-only investment adviser, inside a wealth-management firm, or, less commonly, as a broker-dealer representative, and the fiduciary duty from Step 1 tracks that underlying role every time. Step 1: Understand fiduciary vs suitability The single most important test is the standard your advisor follows. A fiduciary is required by law to act in your best interest, disclose conflicts, and avoid self-dealing. The SEC applies this fiduciary duty to registered investment advisers under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Brokers historically only had to recommend something suitable, a weaker rule that allowed higher-fee products when a cheaper option would also fit. Regulation Best Interest now raises the broker standard, but it is still not the same as fiduciary duty. Ask any advisor in writing which standard covers each of your accounts, and read the firm's Form CRS. Our guide to what a fiduciary is explains which standard applies to advisers, brokers and CFP professionals. Step 2: Compare fee-only, commission, and hybrid How an advisor is paid shapes what they recommend. Fee-only advisors are paid only by you, either as a percentage of assets managed (often around 1% per year), a flat fee, or an hourly rate. This model reduces conflicts because their pay does not depend on which product you buy. Commission-based advisors earn from the products they sell you, like mutual funds, annuities, or insurance. Hybrid advisors can charge both. The SEC recommends comparing fees in actual dollars, not just percentages. A 1% fee on $500,000 is $5,000 a year, which needs to buy real value to be worth it. Step 3: Look for the CFP credential The CFP (Certified Financial Planner) is the most respected credential in personal financial planning. CFP professionals must complete college-level coursework, pass a rigorous exam, meet an experience requirement, and follow a code of ethics. CFP Board rules require them to act as fiduciaries when giving financial advice. Our guide to what a CFP is and what it takes to earn one lists the four certification requirements. Other credentials exist and vary widely in rigor. The SEC warns that professional designations do not all require the same difficulty, and some may indicate product limitations. A CFP with a fee-only fiduciary practice is a strong starting point for most families. If you're sizing up a fund manager rather than hiring a personal planner, see what a CFA charter actually means and how it differs from a CFP. Step 4: Verify the advisor before you hire Never hire an advisor without checking their record. The SEC provides two free tools you should always use. Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) at adviserinfo.sec.gov shows the firm's Form ADV, services, fees, conflicts, and any disciplinary history. FINRA's BrokerCheck at brokercheck.finra.org covers brokers. The SEC also requires most advisors to give you Form CRS, the Customer Relationship Summary. It discloses services, fees, conflicts, and any disciplinary events in plain language. If someone will not send you a Form CRS or ADV, walk away. Step 5: Questions to ask on the first call Bring the same short list to every advisor you interview. Ask: Which standard covers each of my accounts, in writing? How are you paid, exactly, and what will my total annual cost be in dollars? What credentials do you hold, and is one the CFP? Also ask: Who is your typical client, and do they look like me? How often will we meet, and who is my main contact? What happens to my accounts if you leave or retire? A good advisor answers each question directly. A vague or evasive answer is your signal to keep looking. For the full interview script, see our questions to ask a financial advisor . Frequently asked questions How do I choose a financial advisor? Choose a financial advisor by starting with the fiduciary standard, then the fee model, then credentials. A fee-only fiduciary who holds the CFP credential is a strong starting point. Always verify their record on SEC IAPD or FINRA BrokerCheck before you sign anything. What is a fiduciary financial advisor? A fiduciary financial advisor is legally required to act in your best interest. The SEC applies this fiduciary duty to registered investment advisers under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Brokers historically followed a weaker 'suitability' standard, though Regulation Best Interest now raises that bar. What is the difference between fee-only and commission? A fee-only advisor is paid only by you, through a percentage of assets, a flat fee, or an hourly rate. A commission-based advisor is paid by the companies whose products they sell. Fee-only reduces conflicts because the advisor's pay does not depend on which product you buy. What does CFP mean? CFP stands for Certified Financial Planner, the leading credential in personal financial planning. CFP professionals must complete college-level coursework, pass an exam, meet an experience requirement, and follow a code of ethics. CFP Board rules require them to act as fiduciaries when giving financial advice. How do I verify a financial advisor? Verify an advisor using the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) at adviserinfo.sec.gov and FINRA's BrokerCheck at brokercheck.finra.org. Both are free and show the advisor's firm, services, fees, and any disciplinary history. Also request Form CRS and Form ADV before hiring. How much does a financial advisor cost? Costs vary by model. A fee-only advisor may charge about 1% of assets managed per year, a flat annual fee of a few thousand dollars, or an hourly rate. On $500,000, a 1% fee is $5,000 a year, so compare fees in actual dollars, not just percentages. Where can I find a financial advisor? Start with SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) at adviserinfo.sec.gov or FINRA BrokerCheck at brokercheck.finra.org, which let you search for advisors directly by name or firm instead of relying on an ad. The CFP Board also maintains a directory of CFP professionals. Wherever you find candidates, run them through the same verification steps before you hire anyone. What's the difference between a financial advisor and a wealth advisor? Little in regulation, since a wealth advisor usually follows the same fiduciary standard as an investment adviser. The real difference is who they serve: a wealth advisor typically targets higher-net-worth clients and sets a higher account minimum, often $500,000 or more, while a general financial advisor works with a broader range of account sizes. Is a financial coach the same as a financial advisor? Not necessarily. Titles differ, so ask what that specific person provides and verify any registration or designation they claim. A financial advisor who manages a portfolio needs to be registered as an investment adviser or a broker-dealer representative, a different regulatory category entirely.
